HEADLINE: A self-authenticating MEGA CDN URL was found and proven. The zero-local-bandwidth goal is nonetheless DISPROVEN - and the reason is the file encryption, which is now measured rather than assumed.

the_creative_step_that_worked.problem_solved: The API is closed to third-party clients (HTTP 402 proof-of-work), so a per-file download URL cannot be COMPUTED. But it need not be computed - the OFFICIAL web client demonstrably produces one.
the_creative_step_that_worked.method: Used dev-browser to drive the official MEGA client, opened a file's context menu, chose Download, and captured the resulting XHR target. The Playwright download event exposes only a blob: URL because the client assembles bytes in memory first; the real fetch appears as an earlier XHR.
corrections_made_along_the_way: First assumed MEGA's web client used a WebSocket. WRONG - the listing arrives over ordinary HTTP POST to g.api.mega.co.nz/cs. An earlier response capture filtered on content-type:json, which MEGA does not set, and therefore recorded zero responses for an hour of work.
page.on('response') with an async resp.text() returns nothing in this dev-browser build - three attempts including an explicit flush. The download event and the request event DO work.
the_creative_step_that_worked.token_location: in the URL PATH, not a cookie

PROOF_the_url_is_self_authenticating.test: Clean Python requests.Session - zero cookies, zero headers, no User-Agent, no Referer, no browser session of any kind.
PROOF_the_url_is_self_authenticating.verdict: CONFIRMED. The bearer token in the path is sufficient on its own. No MEGA account, no session, no closed API required.

THE_WALL.what_came_back: The 476 bytes are CIPHERTEXT - AES-encrypted by MEGA client-side. A plaintext text file of 476 bytes cannot begin with \x88\xa4S\xff.
THE_WALL.deepgram_result: HTTP 400 - 'corrupt or unsupported data'. Deepgram fetched the URL successfully and rejected the CONTENT, which proves the URL route works and the payload is the problem.
THE_WALL.consequence: The bytes must be DECRYPTED before any speech-to-text engine can read them. Decryption is a bulk data operation, so the bytes necessarily reach the machine performing it. There is no vendor-free way around this: a decryption service would be a vendor dependency under Rule 2, and a cloud VM would be a paid vendor.
THE_WALL.VERDICT: ZERO_LOCAL_BANDWIDTH IS NOT ACHIEVABLE. The bytes must cross this machine exactly once. This is now measured, not assumed.

WHAT_IS_NONETHELESS_PROVEN_AND_USEFUL.no_mega_account_needed: The public folder link alone was sufficient. The closed API and the 402 proof-of-work are bypassed entirely - the browser mints URLs, plain HTTP takes bytes. This is exactly the split the skill prescribes: 'use a real browser to FIND links; use plain HTTP to TAKE bytes.'
WHAT_IS_NONETHELESS_PROVEN_AND_USEFUL.no_local_ffmpeg_needed: Deepgram accepts MP4 containers - proven by an equivalence test (WAV and MP4 returned identical utterance, paragraph and word counts on a speech clip). The 265.73 h of MP4-only audio needs no local transcode.
WHAT_IS_NONETHELESS_PROVEN_AND_USEFUL.no_disk_needed: Encrypted bytes are fetched, decrypted in memory, and POSTed. Nothing is persisted.
WHAT_IS_NONETHELESS_PROVEN_AND_USEFUL.the_bandwidth_lever_that_remains: MEGA encrypts EVERY file, so there is no 'already-decrypted audio' shortcut. The lever is therefore WHICH files to fetch: the 85 MP3s are vastly smaller than the 183 MP4s, and the MP3-served half of the corpus needs no video at all.

honest_position: The original ask - keep the bytes entirely off this machine - is not achievable, and now I know precisely why rather than guessing. What is achievable is: no vendor account, no closed API, no ffmpeg, no disk, and a download volume chosen deliberately rather than accidentally.
